Facts · process · worked example · downloadable

The Deterministic Classifier Lab

Why a fixed table of words and points gives the same answer every time and a Copilot prompt can't be guaranteed to, and how to build, freeze and apply one. A journey from the facts, through the process, to a worked example you can copy.

The short version

  1. A Copilot prompt can't be guaranteed to give the same answer twice. Microsoft's documentation says generative answers aren't deterministic, and published research found variation in LLMs set up to be deterministic. We leave it out and move on (Why Copilot prompts are left out).
  2. A fixed table of words and points can be guaranteed. The same complaint goes in, the same label comes out, and you can check it with a fingerprint of all the answers. A person can write the table (keyword rules), or Python can learn it from complaints that already have the right label.
  3. The method is four moves. (a) Start with correctly labelled complaints. (b) Python builds the table from them. (c) Take new complaints. (d) Apply the frozen table to the new complaints, in Python or in Excel formulas.
  4. Every number on this page comes from a test you can re-run. The complaints are synthetic, and the code has been run in ordinary Python, not yet inside Excel (What was shown, and what wasn't lists what is and isn't shown).
Where the evidence pointsBuild the tables once in Python, using a fixed seed. Freeze them. Apply them to new complaints with Python or with Excel formulas, keep the keyword rules where you want a readable reason, and send complaints the process isn't sure about to a person. On the test data here, the learned table was the most accurate single method and the rules were the easiest to explain (Your options side by side has the figures). This is synthetic data, so measure on your own before relying on it.
Who is "I"?On this page "I" is Claude, the AI that built the data and code and ran every test reported here.
Words you'll meet: TF-IDF, seed, frozen, fingerprint
TF-IDF
A way of turning a complaint into numbers by counting its words, giving more weight to distinctive words than to common ones.
Logistic regression
The step that works out how many points each word should add to each category.
Held-back (test) set
Complaints kept out of the learning on purpose. Because the method has never seen them, scoring it on them shows how it will do on new ones. Also called held-out, unseen or test complaints.
Cell
One box of Python code in Excel, run top to bottom. This page numbers them 1 to 28.
Seed
A number that fixes a random draw, like writing down which names you pulled from a hat. Here the draw is which complaints are held back for testing. It is used when building the table. Applying a finished table to new complaints uses no seed. Plain-English explanation.
Frozen
Saved so it can't change: the same table, the same settings and the same labels every time.
Fingerprint
A short code summarising all of a model's answers. If two runs give the same code, they gave the same answers.

The two tables this page builds

Table A · keyword rulesWords and points a person approves

59 keywords, each worth 1, 2 or 3 points to a category.

e.g. fee adds 2 points to Fees & Charges. The 1 to 3 rating explains who sets the points.

Table B · learned weightsWords and points Python works out

819 words and word pairs, learned from 720 correctly labelled complaints.

e.g. callback adds about 2 points to Customer Service

New complaint→Table A labels it if the evidence is strong→otherwise Table B labels it if it is at least 60% confident→otherwise a person decides

The two tables are separate: the model doesn't produce the rules. Whether you need both is a question the page answers with numbers (Your options side by side).

1Why a Copilot prompt is left out

The claim to test: "if five people run the same agent instructions on the same data, they get exactly the same answer." Here is what the documentation and the research say, and what we do about it.

What is documented

SourceWhat it saysWhat it does and doesn't tell you
Microsoft Learn: FAQ for generative answers (Copilot Studio), under "What are the limitations of generative answers?" "Answers from language models aren't deterministic. Repeating semantically (near) identical questions might yield varying answers, even in new chats." (In plain terms: asking the same thing in nearly the same words can give different answers.) Microsoft states that repeat answers can vary. The page gives no setting for making them repeat. It is about generative answers, so it doesn't measure a classification agent on your data.
Atil et al., "Non-Determinism of 'Deterministic' LLM Settings" (arXiv 2408.04667) Five LLMs, eight tasks, ten runs each, using settings meant to be deterministic. Accuracy varied by up to 15% between runs of the same task, and no model gave consistently repeatable accuracy across all tasks, let alone identical output text. Evidence that "deterministic" settings don't guarantee repeatable answers. It tested models through an API in a research setting, not Copilot Studio, and it is a preprint (not yet peer reviewed).

What follows from that

  • We can say: a Copilot prompt that classifies complaints can't be guaranteed to repeat. The vendor says answers can vary, and the research shows that even settings meant to remove variation don't.
  • We can't say: that it always differs, or by how much on your complaints. Nobody has shown that here, and this page doesn't try.
  • Why that is enough: a process that has to give the same answer every time needs a method where repeating is something you can build and prove. A prompt can't promise it. So we drop it and move on.
Where an AI assistant is still usefulIt can help write the keyword list, or the code, once, offline. A person then reviews and approves it, and from that moment the list is a fixed table. Copilot suggesting keywords and Excel doing the lookups is a sound split, because the non-repeatable step (drafting suggestions) happens once and is checked, and the step that touches your complaints (the lookup) is fixed. The 1 to 3 rating shows how to check suggested keywords against labelled data.

If someone insists

"We tested it five times and got the same answer."

That is evidence about five runs, not a guarantee. The documentation above says varying answers are possible, and the research found variation even under settings meant to prevent it. If the result must be repeatable for audit, "it matched when we tried" is a weaker position than "it cannot differ, and here is the fingerprint".

"Ask Copilot to give a confidence score, or to use a seed."

A confidence score from the same model is another generated answer, so it can vary in the same way. And a prompt can't set a random seed inside the model: a seed is a setting of the software running the model, not something the text of a prompt controls. I found nothing in Microsoft's documentation that offers one for Copilot Studio.

"Then is a trained model any better?"

Yes, once it is built and saved, because it is a table of numbers applied the same way each time. Building it has one random step (the train/test split), which the seed pins. The seed test shows exactly what happens when it isn't pinned.

Every option that gives the same answer every time is some kind of fixed table. They differ in who writes it, who applies it, what you need, and what they cost.

SAS source: SAS Visual Text Analytics features list. It describes custom concepts built from keywords, Boolean operators and regular expressions, categorisation rules, automatic rule generation (BoolRule) and score code. That is the same shape of work as the keyword table and the learned table. Whether it is a good fit for you depends on whether your organisation already has it.

On the 180 complaints held back from training (so none of the methods had seen them):

MethodAnswers (share)Accuracy when it answersOverall accuracy (no answer = wrong)
Exact keywords, formulas (part 1)35.6%82.8%29.4%

"Answers" is the share of complaints given any label. A method that stays silent isn't wrong, but it hasn't done the job either, so read the last column as "what share ended up correctly labelled".

Do I use both rules and the learned table?

In the table below, "model only" still sends complaints under 60% confidence to a person, which is why it differs from the 90.0% figure for the model with no review line.

The numbers say it depends on what you value. These are the 200 new complaints from the worked example, which neither method had seen (Example 5: check the result walks through them). In every row "sent to a person" are complaints the process wouldn't label.

sent to a person accuracy of the rest overall (sent to a person = wrong)
rules first 16 88.6% 81.5%
model first, rules second 16 91.3% 84.0%
model only 29 94.7% 81.0%
  • The learned model alone with no review line (forced to label every complaint) got 90.0% of all 200 right. That is the best single figure here.
  • Rules first, then model (the order used in the worked example) labelled 184 and sent 16 to a person. 71 of the labels came with a readable reason, and 88.6% of the labelled ones were right.
  • Model first, rules second did slightly better (91.3% of those labelled) on the same 16 for review. The difference is a handful of complaints out of 200, so I wouldn't call it decisive.
  • So: use both if you want readable reasons on part of the volume and a person looking at the unclear ones. Use the learned table alone if accuracy is all that matters and you can accept labels with no simple reason. In both cases the answer is the same every time once the tables are frozen. The order is a policy choice, not a technical one.

Choosing between them

  1. No labelled complaints yet, and a short list of well-understood categories: start with the keyword table. Write the keywords, then audit them as soon as you have labelled data.
  2. A few hundred correctly labelled complaints and a wide range of wording: build the learned table. It will find vocabulary nobody listed.
  3. The people applying it can't run Python: build with Python, then apply with formulas.
  4. You already have SAS and people who use it: look at SAS. Treat it as untested here.

3The 1 to 3 rating: who decides, and is it scientific?

Every keyword in a rules table carries a weight of 1, 2 or 3. This page explains what it means, who set it in the example, and how to replace guesswork with evidence.

Three different numbers, kept apartPoints (1 to 3) are per keyword. The 3-and-2 rule (at least 3 points, a lead of at least 2) decides whether the rules label one complaint. The 80% / 60% cut-offs are used once, to turn a keyword's measured reliability into 3, 2 or 1 points. The model's 60% confidence line is a different thing again: below it, the model's answer goes to a person.

What the number means

The weight is points. When a keyword appears in a complaint, it adds its points to its category. Add up the points per category. A category wins only if it has at least 3 points and leads the runner-up by at least 2. Otherwise the rules say nothing and the complaint passes on.

A worked example

"I cannot log in to the app and the password reset never arrives."

Keyword foundCategoryPoints
log inAccount Access3
passwordAccount Access3
resetAccount Access2
appAccount Access1

Account Access scores 9. Nothing else scored. 9 is at least 3, and leads by at least 2, so the label is Account Access, and the matched words are the explanation. You can try your own complaints on Try the keyword scorer.

A 3 means "this word is strong evidence for the category". A 1 means "weak hint". That is a claim about how often the word points to the right category. It can be checked.

Who decided the weights in this example?

I did, by judgement, as a deliberately rough first draft of 59 keywords. It isn't scientific. In real life it would be you, or a colleague who knows the complaints, or an assistant such as Copilot suggesting a list. In every case it is a guess until it is measured.

Checking the guess against labelled data

Cell 18 takes each keyword and, using only the 720 training complaints, counts how many contain it and how often the complaint's true label is the keyword's category. Then it suggests a weight from the evidence: 3 if it was right at least 80% of the time, 2 if at least 60%, otherwise 1. Keywords seen fewer than 8 times get 1, because there isn't enough evidence to trust more.

  • Keywords I gave 3 points were right 75% of the time on average when they appeared. Those I gave 1 point were right 82% of the time. The weights I chose barely track how reliable the words are (correlation -0.17, where 0 means no relationship).
  • Only 11 of my 17 three-point keywords earned a 3 from the evidence.
  • The evidence disagreed with my weight on 29 of 59 keywords: 8 should go down, 21 up.

The least reliable keywords in the table, worst first:

KeywordCategory it adds toWeight a person gaveTimes seen in the 720 training complaintsRight when seenWeight the evidence suggests
log inAccount Access33625%1
on holdCustomer Service33829%1
fraudFraud & Scams33642%1
interest rateFees & Charges21450%1
promisedMis-selling12556%1
feeFees & Charges210560%2
fakeFraud & Scams21861%2
outstandingDelays & Processing21164%2

"Log in" and "fraud" felt like strong signals when I wrote them. Across all 900 labelled complaints, "log in" appears in 52 but only 11 are about Account Access (in the 720 training complaints it appears 36 times, and is right 25% of the time). The rest mention it as a second issue ("...my claim was rejected. I could not log in to check either."), and the true label is the first issue. Real complaints do the same, which is why a word's reliability has to be measured and not assumed.

Does evidence-based weighting help?

Cell 19 re-scores the 180 held-out complaints with the evidence-based weights, at three sets of cut-offs.

answers (share of 180) accuracy when it answers overall accuracy (no answer = wrong)
Your hand-set weights 35.6% 82.8% 29.4%
Evidence weights, cut-offs 90% / 70% 28.9% 90.4% 26.1%
Evidence weights, cut-offs 85% / 65% 33.3% 90.0% 30.0%
Evidence weights, cut-offs 80% / 60% 47.8% 87.2% 41.7%
  • At 80% / 60% the rules answered 47.8% of complaints instead of 35.6%, and were right 87.2% of the time they answered instead of 82.8%. Counting no answer as wrong, that is 41.7% instead of 29.4%.
  • Stricter cut-offs make the rules more accurate and quieter. That is the trade-off: you choose how confident a keyword must be to earn 3 points.
  • Be careful with the best row. I tried three sets of cut-offs and scored them on the test complaints, so the best one is slightly flattering. In real use, choose the cut-offs on a separate validation set, or on the training data, and score the test set once.
  • Better weights can't add words that aren't in the table. Most of the gap to the learned table is coverage, which is why Table B exists.

So, is it scientific?

Partly. The audit is a measurement: how often a keyword is right on correctly labelled data. The cut-offs (80%, 60%) and the minimum of 8 sightings are still judgement calls, and the data must be representative. The fully principled version is the one that doesn't ask anybody to pick cut-offs: logistic regression finds the weights itself by fitting to the labelled complaints. That is Table B.

Can Copilot suggest the keywords while Excel does the lookups?

Yes. Because Copilot would only be drafting a list once, and not labelling complaints, its lack of repeatability doesn't matter for the result. A sound workflow:

  1. Draft. Ask Copilot (or a colleague) for keywords per category. Treat the output as suggestions.
  2. Audit. Run the audit (cell 18) on labelled training complaints. Drop or down-weight keywords that aren't reliable.
  3. Approve. A named person signs off the table and its version (for example rules-v2).
  4. Freeze. Save it as values. From now on Excel formulas do the lookups, and the same complaint always gets the same label.
  5. Review. When the labelled data grows, audit again, and record a new version rather than overwriting.

4The process, step by step

Seven steps. For each one: what it is, why it matters, and how it is done. The worked example then does them in five pages: example 1 is step 1, example 2 is steps 2 and 3, example 3 is steps 4 and 5, example 4 is step 6, and example 5 is step 7 (checking the result).

1 Labelled data→2 Hold back a test set→3 Build the tables→4 Test→5 Freeze→6 Apply to new data→7 Review and maintain

Steps 1 to 5 happen once, or whenever you rebuild. Step 6 happens every time new complaints arrive. The only random choice is in step 2 (which complaints are held back). Training in step 3 has no random step in this setup. Step 6 has none at all.

What "rebuild" means Re-running the steps that create the word-and-points table (the split and the learning, cells 2 to 4) so a new table comes out. It happens in three situations:
  1. You choose to refresh it: more correctly labelled complaints, or the wording of complaints has changed.
  2. Someone re-creates it to check it: a colleague or auditor runs the same cells on the same data and expects the same table.
  3. Excel does it for you: as I understand Python in Excel, its cells recalculate like formulas, so if the cells that build the table are live in the workbook, every recalculation is a rebuild. Without a seed, each rebuild could set aside a different 180 and quietly change some labels. With the seed, it rebuilds the same table. Pasting the finished table or labels as values stops the rebuilding altogether. I haven't tested this inside Excel.

So the seed is insurance for situations 2 and 3, and freezing is what removes situation 3.

The seed: when, where and why, in one place

  • When: once, in step 2, when you split the labelled complaints into the 720 to learn from and the 180 to test on. Nowhere else matters.
  • Where: one line of code, in cell 2: SEED = 42. Cell 2 then passes it to the split as random_state=SEED. (Cell 4 also mentions it, but changes nothing. You can ignore that one.)
  • Why: so that rebuilding the tables from the same data gives the same tables, and you can prove it.
  • Not used: the keyword rules, applying the tables to new complaints (step 6), and Excel formulas. None of them has a random step.
  • If you rebuild later: keep the same number and write it down with the version.

Honest limit: if you build once, save the table as values and never rebuild, the seed has done its job and nothing needs it again. What makes the labels repeat after that is the saved table.

The seed in plain English

The problem. The method learns a list of words and the points each word is worth. To find out whether the list is any good, you test it on complaints it hasn't learned from. So before learning, you set aside 180 of the 900 complaints as a test. The other 720 are what it learns from.

Who picks the 180? The computer, at random, like shuffling 900 cards and dealing off 180. Shuffle again tomorrow and you deal a different 180. Then the list is learned from a different 720, so a word may be worth a little more or less, and a complaint that was a close call can get a different label.

What the seed does. It is a number that tells the computer which shuffle to use. Same number, same shuffle, same 180 set aside, same list of words and points, same labels. Any number works (this page uses 42). What matters is that you keep using it and write it down.

What it doesn't do. Once the list is built and saved, you use it on new complaints by looking up words and adding up points. There is no shuffle in that, so no seed is needed.

Refreshing the table later

When you have more labelled complaints (for example, the ones people decided from the review queue), you rebuild. Doing it properly:

  1. Add the new correctly labelled complaints to the labelled data.
  2. Rebuild with the same seed number and settings, and write down the seed, the date, how many complaints, and a new version name such as v2.
  3. Expect the table to change. Using the same seed does not bring the old table back, because the data is different: a seed fixes the draw from a given set of complaints, and this is a new set. Some borderline labels will change, and that is a new version, not a mistake.
  4. Check v2 against v1 on labelled complaints neither has seen before you switch over.
  5. Keep the old labels frozen. Past batches keep their v1 labels; only new batches get v2.

If you rebuild from exactly the same data, the same seed gives the identical table, and the fingerprint (cell 6) proves it. That is what the seed is for.

Python or Excel formulas? Do I use both?

Both, for different jobs. The question isn't which is better but which step each is good at.

Python (for example Python in Excel)Excel formulas
Good atBuilding: splitting, training, measuring, fingerprinting. Also applying, and fast at any volume.Applying a finished table. Anyone can open, read and audit every formula.
Can't doBe read by people who don't code. Needs the Python environment.Train a model. Handle typos. Scale well: the learned table needs 4.4 million text searches for 900 complaints.
Same answer every time?Yes, with the seed fixed when building, and the table frozenYes, formulas have no random step
How close to each otherThe learned table applied as formulas agreed with the real Python model on 94.0% of the 200 new complaints. It is an approximation: it doesn't remove common words or scale each complaint's word values the way the Python model does.
Two cautionsPython in Excel runs in Microsoft's cloud, so check with your data protection team before using real complaints. And I have tested the code in ordinary Python and the workbook in LibreOffice, not inside Excel, so try both on a copy first.

5Freezing it in place

"Frozen" means tomorrow's 900 labels are the same as today's, and you can prove it. There are four layers. Each one closes a gap the one before it leaves open.

  1. Pin the inputs. The same complaints table, the same rules table, the same settings. Record the row count so a silently changed table shows up.
  2. Pin the randomness. The seed on the train/test split (cell 2). The seed test shows what happens without it.
  3. Record the evidence. Run cell 6 (fingerprint) and cell 13 (run log): date, rules and model versions, seed, row counts, fingerprint and library versions. Keep that row beside the labels.
  4. Pin the outcome. Copy cell 9's 900-row output and use Paste Special, Values onto a sheet called Frozen. The labels are now data rather than a calculation. They can't move when the workbook recalculates, when someone edits the model cell, or when a library update changes a borderline case.
Why layer 4 mattersLayers 1 to 3 make a recalculation reproducible on the same setup. Layer 4 makes the result permanent. If you only do layers 1 to 3 and the library versions change, a borderline label could still move. The fingerprint and run log are how you would notice.

What exactly is frozen?

Two things. The tables (the keyword rules and the learned weights) are the frozen model. The labels for a given batch are the frozen result. Applying a frozen table to new complaints (Example 4: apply to new complaints) needs no seed: the seed only matters while the table is being built.

Checking for drift

Put the frozen labels in the run_1 column of a table called Runs, and a fresh recalculation in run_2. Cell 14 reports the agreement and cell 15 lists any complaint that moved. 100% agreement means nothing has moved.

What freezing does not do

  • It doesn't make new complaints get the same labels as old ones. New data means a new run, so record it as a new version (for example tfidf-lr-v2) rather than overwriting the old one.
  • It doesn't make the labels correct. It makes them repeatable and explainable, so errors can be found and fixed deliberately.
Not tested in ExcelI tested the code in Python, not inside Excel. Paste Special, Values is ordinary Excel and shouldn't depend on Python, but check that it behaves as expected on a copy of your workbook first. In ordinary Python (outside Excel) the stronger version is to train once, save the model file, and only ever load it; the downloadable script does this.

6Example 1 of 5: start with correct data

This is what to do, why, and how. The end result is a workbook with your labelled complaints and your keyword table loaded as Excel tables.

What to doGet complaints that already have the right category

Here: 900 synthetic complaints, 150 in each of 6 categories.

WhyThe learned table copies the answers it is shown

If the labels are wrong, the weights will be wrong. These labels are known to be right because the data is synthetic.

How, in Excel

  1. Download sample_complaints.csv and keyword_rules.csv from Downloads. Also download the two new-complaint files; they are used in Example 4: apply to new complaints and are kept apart on purpose.
  2. In Excel use Data → From Text/CSV to load each file onto its own sheet.
  3. Click inside each dataset, press Ctrl+T to make it a table, and rename the tables on the Table Design tab: Complaints and Rules. Later you will add NewComplaints and Answers the same way.
  4. On a new sheet, click a cell, then Formulas → Insert Python (or type =PY and press Tab). Paste a cell, press Ctrl+Enter, then paste the next one into the cell below. Python in Excel runs cells top to bottom and later cells reuse earlier variables, so keep the order.
  5. For cells that return a table, set the output to Excel Value to see the grid.

7Example 2 of 5: build the tables

Split the data, build the keyword table and audit its weights, then let Python learn the second table.

2a. Hold back a test set

What720 to learn from, 180 locked away

30 of the locked-away complaints per category.

Why, and why a seedThe seed decides which 180

Same seed, same 180 every time. Leave it out and every rebuild learns from a different 720. See the seed in plain English, and The seed test for what happens without it.

2b. Table A: the keyword rules, audited

What: 59 keywords with 1 to 3 points, scored as The 1 to 3 rating explains. Why: they give readable reasons and let a person's knowledge in. How: run the rules (cell 3), audit each weight against the training complaints (cell 18), then see whether the evidence-based weights score better (cell 19).

Result: on the 180 held-back complaints the hand-set rules answered 35.6% of them and were right 82.8% of the time. With evidence-based weights at 80% / 60%: 47.8% answered, 87.2% right. The keyword table is a first draft, so this is the weakest part by design.

2c. Table B: train the model

What: TF-IDF turns each complaint into weighted word and word-pair numbers, and logistic regression works out how many points each one adds to each category. Why: it finds vocabulary a person wouldn't list (819 terms against 59 keywords). How: one cell. Training has no random step in this setup, so the same 720 complaints always give the same table.

Here is your resultTwo tables: A, the keyword rules with audited weights, and B, the learned weights. Both are built on the 720 training complaints only. Neither has been tested yet.

8Example 3 of 5: test it, then freeze it

Measure on the 180 complaints the tables have never seen, prove the build repeats, and save the finished table so it can't change.

3a. Test

Why: the 720 training complaints score 98.8%, which flatters the model. The 180 held back score 85.6%. That is the figure to expect on new complaints, if they look like these. How: cell 5. Reading the numbers explains precision, recall and F1.

3b. Prove it repeats

What: the model is trained from scratch five times and a fingerprint is taken of every label and probability for all 900 complaints. Why: identical fingerprints mean nothing in the build is random once the seed is set. How: cell 6.

3c. Freeze

What: the learned table, exported to a sheet and pasted as values, plus a run log (date, versions, seed, fingerprint). Why: after this the labels can't move when the workbook recalculates or a library updates. How: cells 20 and 13, then Paste Special, Values. Freezing it has the full set of layers.

Here is your resultA frozen table of 819 words and word pairs, six weights each, plus a log line. The seed has done its job: it fixed which complaints were held back while you built. From here on, no seed is needed.

  • The keyword rules labelled 71 complaints and were right on 56 (78.9%).

Which figure is the headline?

There are several, and they answer different questions. 81.5% counts the 16 complaints sent to a person as not yet right. The learned model with no review line labelled all 200 and got 90.0% right, but gives no readable reason for any label and no signal about which ones to double-check. The rules-first pipeline trades some accuracy for readable reasons on 71 labels and a person looking at the unclear ones. Which is better is your policy call. Expect something like 5% to 8% to be sent to a person on data like this (it was 5% of the 900 and 8% of these 200); on your own data it depends on the data and where you set the 60% line.

11Taking it further: the kinds of complaint inside each category

Optional. The tables answer "which category is this complaint?" This extra step answers "what kinds of complaint sit inside each category?", so each bucket becomes something people can read and track.

What it is, in plain words

K-means is a way of sorting items into piles of similar ones without being told what the piles are. You choose how many piles (called K). It turns each complaint into numbers using the same word-counting idea as before, drops K starting points into that space, puts each complaint with its nearest starting point, moves each starting point to the middle of its pile, and repeats until the piles stop changing.

  • What it adds: inside "Fees & Charges" you might see late-payment fees, annual fees and unexpected interest as separate piles.
  • What it isn't: it doesn't use your category definitions, and it doesn't give names. People name the piles. It sits after the classification and doesn't replace it.
  • Where the randomness is: the starting points are chosen at random. A seed fixes them, exactly as it fixes the test set earlier. Once the piles are built and saved, putting a new complaint in a pile is just finding the nearest saved centre. That needs no seed and is the same every time.

Step 1. Classify first, and freeze it

Use the labels you already trust: the frozen tables from the worked example. Complaints sent to a person ("Needs review") are left out, because they have no category yet. Here that leaves 854 of the 900. Piles are built inside each category separately.

A complaint put in the wrong category lands in the wrong bucket and may form an odd pile there. That can help you spot classification errors, but it also means piles are only as good as the classification under them.

Step 2. Choose how many piles (K)

What to do: try several values of K in each category and score each. The score here is the silhouette score: roughly, how much closer each complaint is to its own pile than to the next nearest one. Higher means tighter, more separate piles. Why: there is no single correct K, so you want evidence before you use your judgement. How: cell 24.

  • Averaged over the six categories the score rises from 0.15 at K=4 to 0.26 at K=8 and 0.31 at K=10, then 0.30 at K=12. It rises quickly and then flattens, so about 10 is a sensible stopping point here.
  • A flat curve doesn't tell you the "true" number. It tells you adding more piles stops buying much. It is still your decision. We use K=10.

Step 3. Build the piles and keep them

What to do: run K-means in each category with the seed fixed, and save the word-counter and the centres for each category. Those saved objects are the frozen thing, just as the weights table was earlier. How: cell 25.

Here are the ten piles for one category. The numbers are arbitrary labels. They are not names, and a rebuild can hand the same pile a different number.

category pile complaints top words
Fees & Charges 0 17 unexpected charge, unexpected, statement, charge statement, charge
Fees & Charges 1 23 want refunded, payment fee, refunded, late, late payment
Fees & Charges 2 17 told, monthly, monthly fee, charged, fee told
Fees & Charges 3 14 transaction charges, transaction, charges, explained, charges holiday
Fees & Charges 4 16 billed, annual, annual fee, billed annual, fee agreed
Fees & Charges 5 8 rate, notice, notice costing, rate gone, gone notice
Fees & Charges 6 12 account, taken twice, maintenance, maintenance fee, twice month
Fees & Charges 7 17 time, penalty, hit penalty, hit, penalty charge
Fees & Charges 8 6 lower, costs creeping, costs, creeping balance, creeping
Fees & Charges 9 6 took, took overdraft, overdraft fee, limit, overdraft

Step 4. Work out what is in a pile, and name it

A pile arrives as a number, a size and a list of top words. To understand it, do these four things in order.

  1. Read the top words. The five highest-weighted words and word pairs show what the pile is about. Pile 0 of Fees & Charges has 17 complaints and the top words unexpected charge, unexpected, statement, charge statement, charge.
  2. Read the typical complaints. Cell 26 shows the five complaints nearest the centre. They are the most typical, so they show what the pile means.
  3. Read a couple from the edge. The furthest complaints show how loosely the pile holds together. If they have nothing in common with the typical ones, the pile is a mixed bag.
  4. Write a pile card. A name, a one-line definition, a named owner, and the version, for example: "Unexpected charges on a statement. Customers who find a charge they weren't told about. Owner: complaints team lead. Version: piles-v1."
where distance text
typical 0.69 There is an unexpected charge on my statement of £48. I would like a response in writing.
typical 0.70 There is an unexpected charge on my statement of £60. This is not acceptable.
typical 0.72 Hello, There is an unexpected charge on my statement of £48.
typical 0.73 There is an unexpected charge on my statement of £120. I would like a response in writing.
typical 0.73 There is an unexpected charge on my statement of £120. I would like a response in writing.
edge 0.84 There is an unexpected charge on my statement of £60. I do not think it was explained properly when I bought it.
edge 0.86 I am writing to complain. There is an unexpected charge on my statement of £60. I also spent ages on hold when I called about it. Please sort this out.

Pile 0 of Fees & Charges, with the five most typical complaints and two from the edge. Every one is about an unexpected charge, so "Unexpected charges on a statement" is an honest name for it.

Step 5. Check the piles

In real life you check by reading: take about ten complaints from each pile and see whether two people would put them in the same pile, and whether the name fits. Because this data is synthetic, we also have an answer key: the specific issue behind each complaint (61 issue types, one of them "vague, no specific issue"). How: cell 27 compares the piles with that key.

  • The agreement score averages 0.88 across the six categories (1 is perfect, 0 is no better than chance), and the lowest is 0.80. The average pile is 0.92 one issue type.
  • Be careful what this proves. The synthetic complaints were written from exactly 10 issue types per category, with set wording, so the piles are far cleaner than real complaints would give. It shows the method works when themes are distinct. It doesn't show how clean your own piles will be.

Step 6. Freeze, and put new complaints into the piles

What to do: give each new complaint its category first (cell 21), then the nearest saved pile in that category. Why it repeats: there is no training and no seed, just finding the nearest saved centre. How: cell 28. The table counts the 184 new complaints that received a category, by category and pile.

What happens when you rebuild the piles

  • The numbers can change. Rebuilding with a different seed (7 instead of 42) grouped the complaints almost identically (agreement 0.99 out of 1), but only 11% of complaints kept the same pile number. So "pile 3" is not a stable name.
  • So name piles after you freeze them, and keep the names with the saved centres. Past batches keep their old pile names. Only new batches get the new version.
  • Rebuilding with the same seed and the same data gives the same piles. The seed fixes the starting points.
LimitsThe data is synthetic and tidy. Piles group complaints that use similar words, which isn't always the same as having the same cause. Naming is human judgement and needs an owner. K is a judgement. And I haven't tested these cells inside Excel (K-means comes from scikit-learn, which Microsoft lists among the Python in Excel libraries).

14The same three ideas using only Excel formulas

No Python, no add-ins, no Copilot. Ordinary formulas that work in any modern Excel, in a workbook you can download.

900 complaints plus 200 new ones, 59 keywords, 819 learned terms, every label a formula
How this was checkedI recalculated the workbook in LibreOffice and compared every label with a Python version of the same scoring code. All three formula methods matched it on all 900 complaints. That is a different question from how closely the formula version of the learned weights matches the real TF-IDF model, which is answered in part 3 and is not a perfect match. I have not opened it in Excel itself. The functions used (SUMPRODUCT, SEARCH, INDEX, MATCH, LARGE, TRIM, SUBSTITUTE) are long-standing and need no dynamic arrays, but try it on your own copy first. The learned-weights sheet runs about 4 million text searches, so a full recalculation may take a few seconds.

1. Standard keyword scoring

Three things per complaint: clean the text, add up the weights of every keyword found (one column per category), then pick the winner only if it is strong and clearly ahead. The two thresholds sit in cells Rules!H1 and Rules!H2, so anyone can see and change them. Categories are listed in priority order, which makes MATCH break ties the same way every time.

Step 1: clean the text (column D). Lowercase it, turn punctuation into spaces, trim, and pad with a space at each end so that "fee" cannot match inside "feel".

=" "&TRIM(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(SUBSTITUTE(LOWER(B2),"."," "),","," "),"'"," "),"’"," "),"!"," "),"?"," "),";"," "),":"," "),"-"," "),"("," "),")"," "),"""", " "),"£"," "),"&"," "),"/"," "),"%"," "))&" "

Step 2: score one category (E2, filled across E to J and down). The pattern column in Rules is the keyword with a space either side.

=SUMPRODUCT((Rules!$A$2:$A$60=E$1)*Rules!$C$2:$C$60*ISNUMBER(SEARCH(Rules!$D$2:$D$60,$D2)))

Step 3: choose the label (K2).

=IF(OR(MAX(E2:J2)<Rules!$H$1,MAX(E2:J2)-LARGE(E2:J2,2)<Rules!$H$2),"No label",INDEX($E$1:$J$1,MATCH(MAX(E2:J2),E2:J2,0)))

2. Fuzzy keyword scoring, as far as formulas can take it

Excel has no built-in fuzzy matching function. What formulas can do is stem matching: match the start of a word, so a keyword like charge also catches charged, charges and charging. Only one formula changes. A second pattern column in Rules (E) trims the last two letters from single keywords of six letters or more, and the scoring formula points at it instead.

=IF(OR(ISNUMBER(SEARCH(" ",B2)),LEN(B2)<6)," "&B2&" "," "&LEFT(B2,LEN(B2)-2))
=SUMPRODUCT((Rules!$A$2:$A$60=L$1)*Rules!$C$2:$C$60*ISNUMBER(SEARCH(Rules!$E$2:$E$60,$D2)))
  • What it handles: endings and word forms.
  • What it can't handle with formulas: typos such as chrage. That needs an edit-distance comparison. The options are Microsoft's separate Fuzzy Lookup add-in (which has to be installed, and which isn't the same thing as a formula), or the Python in Excel version in cell 17 (Python in Excel: all 28 cells).
  • The risk: stems also catch unwanted words. This is why I only stem keywords of six letters or more. Stemming a short keyword like app would match "approve" and "apple".

3. The model's learned weights, run as a lookup

This is a second table, separate from the hand-written keyword rules above. This is the part that matters for the question of what training adds. The frozen TF-IDF + logistic regression model is a table: every word or word pair it learned, with one weight per category. Exported to a sheet called Terms (819 rows, 6 weight columns, plus an intercept row), the scoring is the same shape as the keyword scorer, with learned weights in place of hand-written ones.

=SUMPRODUCT(ISNUMBER(SEARCH(" "&Terms!$A$3:$A$821&" ",$D2))*Terms!B$3:B$821)+Terms!B$2
=INDEX($S$1:$X$1,MATCH(MAX(S2:X2),S2:X2,0))

This is an approximation of the Python model, not a copy. It matches words as they are written, while the Python model first removes common words and scales each complaint's word values. The two agree on 93.9% of the held-out complaints and on 92.2% of all 900. Training itself (working out the weights) still needs Python or another tool. Formulas only apply the finished table.

The results, side by side

On the 180 held-out complaints (the ones the model never saw). Use these rows for any comparison. On the 720 complaints the table was learned from, the formula version scores 91.5% (the Python model scores 98.8%), which flatters both.

MethodAnswers (share)Accuracy when it answersOverall accuracy (no answer = wrong)
Exact keywords, formulas (part 1)35.6%82.8%29.4%

4. Applying the frozen tables to 200 new complaints

The workbook also has three more sheets: NewComplaints (the 200 new complaints), Answers (their true categories) and New, which applies the exact keyword table and the learned Terms table to each new complaint with the same formulas as above. It is the formula route through Example 4: apply to new complaints and Example 5: check the result. Nothing is trained and nothing is random: change the new complaints and the labels recalculate, and the same complaints always give the same labels.

  • The exact keyword table labelled 35.5% of the new complaints and was right on 78.9% of those.
  • The learned table labelled every complaint and was right on 90.0%. It agreed with the real Python model on 94.0%.
  • Rules first, then the learned table when the rules are silent: 86.0%.

All three were recalculated in LibreOffice and checked against Python: the keyword formulas matched on every complaint, and the learned-table formulas matched the Python version of the same lookup on every complaint.

Have we gone wrong? Is there a gap?

A fair challenge, so here is the straight answer. The result stands, but the story I told around it needed tightening.

What we might have impliedWhat the evidence supports
"Frozen TF-IDF with a seed has magic that keyword rules lack."The useful ingredient is a weighted word list built from labelled examples. Once built, it can run as formulas (above), at the same accuracy on the held-out set (85.6%). Nothing about it needs a clever algorithm at run time.
"The seed is what freezes it."The seed only decides which complaints are held back for testing. Training itself has no random step here (The seed test, experiment C). What actually freezes the behaviour is the table of weights. If you save that table, the seed no longer matters for running it.
"Rules score 29.4%, the classifier 85.6%."Partly an artefact of a deliberately thin 59-keyword first draft that declines to answer most complaints. The fairer comparison is a lookup built from the same labelled data, and that is what the Terms sheet is. A person extending the keyword list for long enough would close much of the gap.
"Determinism is the classifier's advantage."Determinism belongs to any fixed table, written by a person or learned by a machine. It is the difference between those and an LLM prompt that this page is really about.
What the classifier genuinely addsIt builds and weights a far larger word list than a person would write (819 against 59), it picks up word pairs, and it does this in seconds from labelled examples. That saves labour and finds vocabulary nobody thought of. It also learns junk from repeated boilerplate, so the list needs a human read before anyone relies on it.
Limits of this whole comparisonThe data is synthetic. Complaints in the real world are messier, labels are less clean, and the gap in either direction could be bigger or smaller. This page shows what can be pinned and how a fixed table behaves. It doesn't measure Copilot.

What this means for the argument

Safe to say
"The thing that gives you the same answer every time is a fixed table of words and weights. You can write the table by hand, learn it from labelled examples, or do both. Either way it runs as ordinary formulas and gives the same label on every recalculation. An LLM prompt isn't a fixed table, and nothing in the documentation guarantees it behaves like one."
Avoid
"TF-IDF is the answer and keyword lookups can't compete." On this data a lookup built from labelled examples does well and a hand-written draft does badly, and that gap is about effort and coverage, not about magic.

Read used_for before you quote any accuracy720 of the 900 complaints were used to teach the model. On those it gets 98.8% right, because it has effectively seen the answers. On the 180 it had never seen it gets 85.6%. Only the second number tells you how it will do on new complaints, in the same way a student's score on the practice paper they revised from says little about the real exam. (Both figures are the model's own labels, before the review queue.)

Run through the full pipeline, the 180 test complaints came out like this: 165 were labelled automatically and 89.1% of those were right (147 of 165), and 15 were sent to a person.

Rules versus TF-IDF: what is actually different in the output

Keyword rulesTF-IDF + logistic regression
Gives a label forOnly the complaints where a strong, clear match exists (64 of the 180 test complaints)Every complaint: it always has a best guess plus a confidence
Accuracy where it speaks82.8% (on the complaints it labelled)89.1% on those same complaints; 85.6% across all 180
Why did it choose that?You can read the exact words that matchedIt learned word weights from examples. It can't give you a single reason you could write on a file.

What changes the outputEditing the keyword tableChanging the training data, the settings or the train/test split

When the two methods disagree

On the 64 test complaints where the rules fired, the model gave the same label on 50. On the other 14 they disagreed: the model was right 9 times, the rules 5 times, and neither was right 0 times. Four real examples:

(65% confident)		Rules
Why these disagreements are mostly two-issue complaintsIn this synthetic data the "true" label is the first issue mentioned. Keyword counting can't know which issue comes first or matters most. Real complaints have the same problem, so decide in advance what counts as the main issue, or let a person decide whenever a complaint mentions two categories.

Why the pipeline puts rules first anyway. Rules can show their working. In this run the model was more accurate than the rules on the same complaints (89.1% against 82.8%), so rules-first buys explainability at some cost in accuracy. You could reverse the order, or accept a label only when both agree and send everything else to review. That is a policy choice, not a technical one.

Your turnEdit the keywords in the Rules table and re-run cells 3, 7, 8 and 9. The 1 to 3 rating explains how to choose the weights. Watch how many complaints the rules claim and how often they are right.

17Reading the numbers

What the figures in cells 2, 5 and 6 mean, with the real numbers from this run.

Train 720, test 180

There are 900 complaints, 150 in each of the 6 categories. Cell 2 sets aside 20% (180) and keeps 80% (720).

  • Train (720): the complaints the model learns from. Think of them as the revision notes.
  • Test (180): complaints locked away until the end. The model has never seen them, so scoring it on them is a fair exam.
  • Why it matters: any model can look brilliant on data it has already learned. The test score is the only one that predicts real-world performance.
  • Why 30 per category: the split is "stratified", so each category gets exactly 30 of the 180 test places. No category is accidentally missing from the exam.
  • What the seed does: it decides which 180 complaints are held back. The same seed gives the same 180 every time.

Precision, recall, F1 and support

Cell 5 produces one row per category. Here is what each column means, using the Fraud & Scams row as the worked example.

Support (30)
How many real Fraud & Scams complaints were in the test set. It tells you how many examples each row is based on. Here it is 30 for every category, so the rows are equally trustworthy.
Precision (0.92)
"When the model says Fraud, how often is it right?" It labelled 25 complaints as fraud and 23 really were: 23 / 25 = 0.92. Low precision means a pile of wrongly flagged complaints.
Recall (0.77)
"Of the real fraud complaints, how many did it find?" There were 30 and it found 23: 23 / 30 = 0.77. The 7 it missed were labelled Account Access (3), Delays & Processing (2), Mis-selling (2). Low recall means real cases slipping through.
F1 (0.84)
A single score that combines precision and recall (their harmonic mean). It sits closer to the lower of the two, so you can't hide poor recall behind good precision.
Accuracy (85.6%)
The simplest one: 154 correct out of 180.
Macro and weighted average
The average across the six categories. They are identical here because every category has the same support. With uneven categories they would differ.

Which matters more? It depends on the cost of a mistake. For fraud you probably care most about recall (don't miss real cases). For a team with limited review time you may care more about precision (don't flood them with false alarms).

Rows are the true category, columns are what the model said. The highlighted diagonal is correct; everything else is a mistake.

What the five runs mean

Cell 6 trains the model from scratch five times and computes a fingerprint: a short code that summarises every prediction and every probability for all 900 complaints. If any single label or probability differed, the code would change.

  • What it shows: five fresh trainings on the same 720 complaints with the same settings gave identical results. Nothing in training or prediction is random.
  • What it doesn't show: that the model is accurate, that it would match after you change the data or the split (experiment B below does exactly that), or that it matches on every machine. It matched across the two library versions I tested, but other versions could differ, so record the fingerprint alongside the version.

All 900 complaints, without the seed

Cell 11 is the seedless version of cell 9: the same pipeline and the same 900 complaints, retrained with no seed on the split. It sits next to the seeded labels so every change is visible. The table below is one run of it. 40 of the 900 final labels differ from the seeded run. I then ran cell 11 a second time with nothing changed, and 50 labels differed from the first seedless run.

Your own run in Excel will give a different table

Filter changed_vs_seeded to True to see only the complaints whose label moved. Rows highlighted in amber are the ones that changed.

  • Neither run is "the" right one. Of the 40 complaints whose label changed, the seeded run was right on 21 and the seedless run on 16. The point is that they disagree about the same complaints.
  • The flips happen on borderline complaints. In the seeded run, the complaints that later changed had an average model confidence of 67%, against 88% for the ones that never changed.
  • Rule-labelled complaints never change. The keyword rules don't depend on the split, so every flip comes from the model.

What the summary experiment shows

  • A. Seed 42 everywhere: one fingerprint, the same accuracy and zero differences, five times out of five.
  • B. No seed on the split: 5 different fingerprints in 5 runs. Test accuracy ranged from 82.8% to 90.6%, and between 40 and 54 of the 900 complaints received a different label from the baseline.
  • C. No seed on the classifier only: nothing changed at all. With scikit-learn's default solver, logistic regression has no random step, so the seed in cell 4 was harmless insurance and not what made the result repeatable. I'd assumed it mattered; the experiment says otherwise.
  • D. No seeds at all: 5 different fingerprints in 5 runs, the same behaviour as B.

Why leaving out the split seed changes the answer

Without a seed, each run picks a different random 180 complaints to hold back. The model then learns from a different 720, so its word weights shift slightly, and complaints sitting on the border between two categories tip the other way. The accuracy also moves partly because each run is marked on a different exam paper. Quote the seed whenever you quote an accuracy figure.

Why this matters if nobody retrains each timeIn normal use you wouldn't retrain on every run. The seed matters when you, or a colleague, rebuild the model: without it, the rebuilt model can label some borderline complaints differently from the one you used before. Saving the finished model, or its table of weights, is what removes the problem for good.
The important distinctionHere the variation comes from a choice you made (a random split), and you can switch it off with a seed. Once the split is fixed, the model gives the same answer every time. With an LLM prompt there is no equivalent dial in your hands: the randomness sits inside the model and its serving infrastructure, so as far as I could find there is no documented way to pin it from your side.

What it shows

  • Rule-labelled complaints never change. 296 out of 296 matched, by construction.
  • Confident model decisions are stable. Among complaints the seeded model was 90% or more sure about, 0 of 371 changed. At 80 to 90%, 5 of 98 changed.
  • The movement sits where the model was unsure. At 60 to 80% confidence, 23 of 89 changed. Among complaints that were already sent to review (under 60%), 12 of 46 changed. Overall, 87.5% of all the changes were on complaints the seeded model was under 80% confident about.
  • Many differences are about the review line, not the category. Of the 40 changes, 25 were a complaint moving into or out of "Needs review" (the model crossing the 60% confidence line), and 15 were a real swap from one category to another. The first kind is less harmful, because a person looks at it anyway. The second kind is a confident label that moved.
What this means for "same result every time"With the seed pinned, all 900 labels are identical on every run. Without it, a small and predictable group of borderline complaints move, and a second unseeded run moved a different small group (50 labels differed from the first). The size is modest. The important part is that nothing tells you in advance which complaints will move unless the seed is fixed.

20"Isn't this just a fuzzy scored lookup?"

A fair question, and the honest answer starts with "partly, yes". Here is exactly where the two are the same and where they differ.

The short versionBoth work the same way at the final step: look at the words in the complaint, add up points for each category, and pick the highest total. A scored keyword lookup and a TF-IDF classifier are close cousins. The difference is who writes the list of words and the points. In a lookup, a person writes them. In the classifier, the computer works them out by studying complaints that people have already labelled. After training, both are fixed tables that give the same answer every time. In this demo they are two separate tables: the keyword rules are written by a person, and the model does not produce them.

An everyday way to see it

Scored lookupA sorting clerk with your cheat sheet
  • You write: "if you see fee, give Fees 2 points; if you see locked, give Account Access 3 points"
  • The clerk follows it to the letter
  • Anything not on the sheet scores nothing
Fuzzy lookupThe same clerk, a bit more forgiving
  • Still your cheat sheet
  • Now also accepts near-spellings: charged or chrage counts as charge
  • A word that isn't on the sheet in any spelling still scores nothing
Trained classifierA clerk who writes the cheat sheet himself
  • Reads 720 complaints that people have already labelled
  • Writes his own sheet of 819 words and word pairs, each with its own points
  • Then follows that sheet to the letter

Fuzzy matching helps with spelling. Training helps with vocabulary you didn't think to list. They solve different problems.

Side by side

Scored keyword lookup (exact or fuzzy)TF-IDF + logistic regression
Who writes the word listA person. Here: 59 keywords.The training step. Here: 819 words and word pairs.
Who sets the pointsA person's judgement ("fee = 2").Arithmetic on the labelled examples. A word that appears mostly in one category and rarely elsewhere earns more points for it.
Word pairsOnly if you write them out.Learns them automatically ("unexpected charge", "hold cut").
A word nobody thought to listScores nothing. Fuzzy matching only helps if it's a near-spelling of a listed word.Counts, if it appeared in the training complaints.
Common filler wordsIgnored unless you list them.Automatically down-weighted (the "TF-IDF" part of the name).
What you need to startDomain knowledge and time.A few hundred correctly labelled complaints. Poor labels give a poor model.
Explaining one labelEasy: "it contained these keywords".Possible but harder: "these learned words added up to the highest total". Some learned words look odd (see below).
Same answer every time?Yes, once the table is versioned.Yes, once the split seed is fixed and the model is frozen (The seed test and Freezing it).

Does a fuzzy lookup close the gap? A real test

Cell 17 runs this on the 180 held-out complaints, with the same scoring rules as cell 3. Three ways of making the lookup more willing to answer are included, so the comparison is fair to the lookup.

answers (share of 180) accuracy when it answers overall accuracy (no answer = wrong)
Exact keywords (cell 3) 35.6% 82.8% 29.4%
Exact keywords, answer whenever any match 86.7% 73.7% 63.9%
Fuzzy keywords, strict (0.85) 36.7% 84.8% 31.1%
Fuzzy keywords, loose (0.75) 50.6% 76.9% 38.9%
TF-IDF + logistic regression 100.0% 85.6% 85.6%
  • Fuzzy spelling barely moves it. The strict version answers 36.7% instead of 35.6% of complaints. The words in the missing complaints weren't spelled wrongly. They simply weren't on the list.
  • Loosening the match answers more, but gets more wrong. Near-matches start catching words that merely look similar.
  • Making the exact lookup answer whenever any keyword matches gets to 86.7% coverage at 73.7% accuracy, still below the classifier's 85.6%.
Read this fairlyThe keyword table here is a 59-keyword first draft, and the data is synthetic. A person who keeps adding keywords would narrow this gap, and on real complaints the size of the gap could be larger or smaller. What the test does show is the direction: spelling tolerance isn't the missing ingredient. Coverage of vocabulary is, and that is what training supplies.

A person reviewing this table would strike them out. A classifier will learn this kind of artefact from any real data that has repeated phrases, which is the main cost of the approach.

So what do you say?

A good reply to "do a fuzzy scored lookup then"
"That's a legitimate approach, and it's deterministic too. The two are close relatives: both add up word evidence. The difference is that a lookup only knows the words someone wrote down, while a trained classifier writes its own, much longer list from labelled examples. Fuzzy matching only fixes spelling, and on our test it hardly changed the result. Either approach gives the same answer every time once it's pinned, which was the point."
A practical middle route
"Train the model, read its highest-weighted words, strike out the junk, and keep the good ones as a human-approved keyword table. You get a lookup that is fully explainable and that started from evidence rather than guesswork. Compare it with the model on a held-out set before trusting it."
Avoid
"The classifier is just better." On a small, clean, well-understood problem a maintained lookup can be the better choice, because anyone can read and defend it. The classifier earns its place when wording is wider than anyone can list.

21What was shown, and what wasn't

What the evidence supports

  • A Copilot prompt can't be guaranteed to repeat. Microsoft's documentation says generative answers aren't deterministic, and published research found variation under settings meant to prevent it (Why Copilot prompts are left out).
  • A fixed table of words and points repeats. Five retrains gave identical fingerprints. 200 new complaints run through the frozen tables get the same labels every time, with no seed involved in applying them (Example 4: apply to new complaints).
  • The only random step is in building. Without a seed on the train/test split, five retrains each changed between 40 and 54 of the 900 labels compared with the seeded baseline (The seed test, experiment B). A single separate seedless run on that page changed 40. These counts differ each time the experiment is re-run, which is the point. Training itself had no random step.
  • Hand-set 1 to 3 weights need checking. Mine tracked reliability poorly (correlation -0.17), and weights set from labelled data helped at one of the three cut-offs I tried (80% / 60%, which I chose using the test complaints, so it is slightly flattering). At the two stricter cut-offs overall accuracy was lower than the hand-set weights (The 1 to 3 rating).
  • The learned table covered more. On the 180 held-back complaints it was right on 85.6% (from one split; across five no-seed splits test accuracy ranged from 82.8% to 90.6%), against 29.4% for the hand-set keywords counting silence as wrong (Your options side by side).
  • The learned table can be applied with formulas. It agreed with the Python model on 94.0% of the new complaints (Formulas-only workbook).
  • Repeatable is not correct. 21 of the 184 automatically labelled new complaints were wrong, and will be wrong every time. Because they repeat, they can be found and fixed (Example 5: check the result).

What it doesn't show

  • How much Copilot varies on your data. It wasn't run. The page says only that repetition can't be guaranteed.
  • Your accuracy. The complaints are synthetic and tidy, and written from templates, so some accuracy may come from boilerplate phrases the model picked up (the learned-terms table includes some junk). Measure on a labelled sample of your own.
  • That any of it works inside Excel. The Python cells ran in ordinary Python, and the formula workbook was recalculated in LibreOffice and matched Python on every complaint. Neither has been opened in Excel. Try both on a copy first.
  • That SAS (or any other tool) behaves the same. Its features page lists the same kinds of tool; I haven't tested it.
  • That the learned table beats a carefully maintained keyword table in general. Only that it did on this data against a first draft.
  • The best order or thresholds. The 60% confidence line, the 3/2 scoring thresholds and the rules-first order are policy choices.

Sources

  • Microsoft Learn: FAQ for generative answers (Copilot Studio)
  • Atil et al., Non-Determinism of "Deterministic" LLM Settings, arXiv 2408.04667
  • SAS Visual Text Analytics features list
Built as a single self-contained file: no server, no build step, no external libraries, so it works on GitHub Pages or any shared machine. All data is synthetic.
